structure.title: Book I · A quarrel with a longer history
structure.text: Disputes over allies and colonies draw Athens and Sparta toward war. Delegates argue about treaties and injuries that can be named in public. Thucydides puts alongside them a quieter explanation about growing power and the fear it causes.

structure.title: Books II–IV · What war does inside a city
structure.text: An invasion, a funeral speech and an epidemic put radically different pictures of Athens in close succession. Revolts elsewhere force the Athenians to debate what an empire may do to subjects it still needs to govern.

structure.title: Books V–VII · A peace and a voyage
structure.text: An uneasy peace leaves allies manoeuvring for advantage. At Melos, overwhelming force changes the terms of a negotiation. The Sicilian expedition then carries the Athenians far from home, with distances and supplies now working on a different scale.

structure.title: Book VIII · The war outlasts its account
structure.text: Persian money, shifting alliances and a constitutional struggle within Athens remake the field. The surviving history breaks off with campaigns under way, leaving readers inside the uncertainty that the speeches so often try to master.

people.name: Pericles
people.role: A leader asking citizens to endure
people.text: He argues that Athens can survive losses to land if it preserves its naval strength. For a family watching invaders destroy its home, the distinction between a city's resources and everything worth defending carries an immediate cost.

people.name: Nicias and Alcibiades
people.text: One warns against the commitment, the other sees opportunity. The assembly's enthusiasm can alter the meaning of either speech. Even a warning about the scale of the resources needed may start sounding like a plan.

context.title: What kind of record is a speech?
context.text: Thucydides explains the difficulty of recovering exact words. The speeches stage what the circumstances called on a speaker to say while aiming to preserve the sense of the argument. Their arrangement lets competing accounts of necessity confront each other.

notice.text: Watch for the second assembly at Mytilene.
notice.why: An order has already gone out when the Athenians reconsider it. The time a ship needs to cross the water gives political repentance a deadline almost painfully exact.

notice.text: Compare a city's self-description with its behaviour under strain.
notice.why: The funeral speech celebrates Athens as an education for others. The plague narrative follows people through damaged routines of burial and care, letting proximity do some of the historian's most searching work.

opening: Athens has wealth, ships, and good reasons to believe its power makes it safer. Sparta finds that power increasingly difficult to tolerate. Thucydides follows the war between them into assemblies where persuasive speeches become military orders and decisions made in fear acquire the language of necessity. He records plague, civil strife, and calculations in which another city's survival is negotiable. The unnerving force comes from recognising competent people, familiar arguments, and institutions under pressure, producing outcomes that almost nobody would have chosen at the beginning.
